title: The Causality Fallacy in Counterfactual Bias Mitigation
text:
Counterfactual Fairness represents an ideal standard for detecting bias, proposing that an algorithmic decision should remain unchanged if only a protected attribute were altered (e.g., gender or ethnicity), assuming all other underlying causes remained constant. This method aims to move beyond mere statistical association by invoking a causal framework.

The primary ethical blind spot lies in the assumption of perfect epistemic access: modeling counterfactuality requires knowledge of the true, underlying causal graph that generated the data. Real-world systems are characterized by undocumented feedback loops and unmeasured confounders; therefore, determining which variables truly drive an outcome versus those merely correlating with it remains an intractable philosophical and technical dilemma.

Consequently, focusing heavily on proving counterfactuality can create a misleading sense of safety. The inability to fully map the causal structure means that algorithmic 'fairness' defined by counterfactual modeling may simply replace one form of bias (statistical correlation) with another (over-reliance on simplifying—and potentially inaccurate—causal assumptions), thereby setting an impossibly high and ethically precarious deployment boundary.
